newsitem.title: USA: New York appeals ruling on reservation taxes.
newsitem.headline: New York appeals ruling on reservation taxes.

text.p: New York state, which was ordered by a state judge to start collecting taxes on cigarettes and gasoline sold on Indian reservations within 120 days, has appealed the ruling though it plans to meet the deadline.

Mike McKeon, a spokesman for Gov. George Pataki, explained that the governor prefers to resolve the issue through talks with the Native Americans, which are continuing. But if an agreement is not reached by the end of the deadline, then the state will start collecting taxes.
"It's the same timeframe the governor had in mind originally," said McKeon, explaining Pataki had been planning to conclude the negotiations with the Native Americans around the end of the year.

About 3,000 convenience stores, located throughout New York state, won their suit in mid-August to force it to collect the taxes, saying that the state's failure to do so gave the reservations an unfair competitive advantage.

Stores that are located within 30 miles of the reservations were being undercut on the prices they charge by more than 20 cents per gallon of gasoline, while some reservations were selling cigarettes for as low as $5.60 a carton, the plantiffs' attorney has said.
David Cherubin of Crane, Kelley, Green & Parente in Albany, who represents the convenience stores, last week said that the state had told him it planned to file an appeal.

A spokesman for the state attorney general, Dennis Vacco, said the state now has filed the appeal because it believes the judge's decision was too broad, according to Marc Carey, a spokesman for Vacco.

"We feel the remedy is overbroad," Carey said, referring to the ruling by State Supreme Court Judge Joseph Harris, who held that the state would have to stop collecting excise and sales taxes at other sites if it did not meet his deadline.

Further, the spokesman pointed to progress in the talks between the Pataki Administration and the Native Americans. "We feel we have been making steady progress. At this point, to have a judge come in and impose a decision is problematic," Carey added.
